records.name: Bayern
records.current_summary:
Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German has been prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration in Bavaria, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities. Coverage notes critics dismissing the measure as symbol politics while recording its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with.

Bavaria is also a partner — with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt — in a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change: an organised state-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter, which critics see as restricting how trans and intersex people use the right.

sources.claim: Tagesschau report on Bavaria's gender-language ban: from 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German is prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 and a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities; critics in the coverage dismiss it as symbol politics while noting its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom.

Antenne Bayern report on the Bundesrat initiative by several Länder — Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt, with Bavaria a partner — to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change, i.e. an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Germany
sources.claim: National framework page applying to Bavaria. Adults have been able to change legal gender since 1980; the Self-Determination Act (Cabinet-approved August 2023; Bundestag vote 374-251 on 12 April 2024) lets adults over 18 change first name and gender by self-determination with three months' notice, in force since 1 November 2024. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods/services, though the page notes some protections vary by region. Supplies the federal legal baseline inside which Bavaria's own measures (the gender-language ban and the Länder push to tighten the SBGG) operate.

sources.title: Selbstbestimmungsgesetz
sources.claim: German Wikipedia article on the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), the federal law Bavaria's Bundesrat initiative sought to tighten. It passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 (374-251, 11 abstentions) and the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, was gazetted 21 June 2024; changes could be registered from 1 August 2024 and took effect 1 November 2024. Adults declare the change themselves before the registry office; 14-17 year-olds need a guardian's (or the family court's) consent; for under-14s only the guardian can declare, and a three-month waiting period applies with a one-year lockout after a change. The article also records the Bundesrat's 20 October 2023 criticism that the draft let parents decide under-14 gender-entry changes 'without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare' - exactly the contested point behind the Bavarian-led tightening initiative this record covers.

records.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
records.current_summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder — with Sachsen and Thüringen — that brought a Bundesrat initiative (reported June 2026) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act on legal gender change, proposing an 'abuse review' mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention. The trigger cited is the 'Fall Liebich' — a convicted far-right extremist whose legal gender was changed after sentencing.

The initiative is an attempt, not a change: it is backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, and runs against a scheduled federal evaluation of the SBGG that the family ministry is conducting and whose SPD-led ministries consider the existing law sufficient. No standing administrative ban or documented street-attack pattern specific to this state was identified in the research pass.
records.current_localsOnly: The SBGG initiative targets the legal gender-change/civil-registry procedure — machinery a visitor never uses; its visitor-facing weight is climate signalling only.

sources.claim: dpa report (updated 2 June 2026): Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thüringen bring a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, proposing an "abuse review" mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention, triggered by the Fall Liebich; backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, while the federal family ministry runs a scheduled SBGG evaluation.

sources.title: German controversy surrounds jail term for transgender far-right extremist - BBC News
sources.claim: BBC News reports (20 August 2025) that Marla-Svenja Liebich, then Sven Liebich, was sentenced in July 2023 by the Halle District Court in Saxony-Anhalt to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult, and changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office under Germany's Self-Determination Act at the end of 2024. The article records the ensuing controversy - the chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Saxony-Anhalt that Liebich would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison, while German outlets including Der Spiegel questioned the change's seriousness - and notes Liebich also lost a case against journalist Julian Reichelt at Berlin Regional Court. This grounds in Saxony-Anhalt the 'Fall Liebich' that the record identifies as the trigger for its Bundesrat initiative.

sources.title: Germany: Gender switch neo-Nazi sent to men's prison - DW
sources.claim: DW reports (16 July 2026) that Marla-Svenja Liebich, legally registered as a woman since 2025, was transferred to a men's prison (Zeithain, Meissen district) after being extradited from the Czech Republic, with prison management saying the decision prioritised the safety of women at the Chemnitz facility. It recalls that Liebich was sentenced to 18 months in July 2023, organised far-right demonstrations since 2014 including many on Halle's central market square, was arrested in the Czech Republic in April 2026, and that a court has yet to decide whether the changes can be reversed. This documents the outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt-linked case behind the record's initiative, including the still-open question of reversing SBGG-based changes.

records.name: Thüringen
records.current_summary:
Thüringen's Landtag exhibits formal, multi-layered hostility to gender policy: an AfD fraction motion demands consistent implementation of a ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools, asserting schools must not be "a socio-political experimental field"; a draft law titled "Thüringer Gesetz zur Beendigung gleichstellungspolitischer Maßnahmen" proposes to dismantle the Land's existing equality-policy machinery, arguing that current law "regularly violates the principle of equal opportunity." Thüringen is also a partner in the Sachsen/Sachsen-Anhalt June 2026 Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal SBGG. The dossier characterises the parliament as "formally hostile to gender policy."

National score is 0.71. Thüringen sits 0.06 below: the equality-dismantling bill is the most consequential institutional signal in this dossier for a visitor — if enacted, a trans person reporting an incident would find no Land-level equality apparatus. The gender-language motion compounds this at the administrative interface. Compared to Sachsen-Anhalt (0.68), Thüringen goes beyond tightening one federal law to actively removing the entire state equality framework; compared to Brandenburg (0.66), the threat is legislative and institutional rather than physical but arguably more pervasive for a visitor's access to recourse. Compared to Bayern (0.67), Thüringen's hostility extends to dismantling protection machinery rather than restricting expression vocabulary.
records.current_localsOnly: The SBGG-tightening role concerns the legal gender-recognition procedure — resident-facing; a visitor never applies to it. The equality-machinery and school-language measures are visitor-facing at administrative and reporting interfaces.

sources.claim: Thuringian Landtag document: AfD fraction motion "Keine Gendersprache an Thüringer Schulen" demanding the Landtag's existing ban on gender-inclusive language in schools be consistently implemented, asserting schools must not be a socio-political experimental field.

Antenne Bayern / dpa (02.06.2026): Thüringen co-signs the Sachsen/Sachsen-Anhalt initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after the 'Liebich case' — anti-abuse amendments framed alongside stronger trans/inter recognition.

sources.title: Landtagswahl in Thüringen 2024
sources.claim: The 1 September 2024 Thuringian state election made the AfD Thüringen, classified by the state's constitution-protection authorities as a right-wing extremist party, the strongest force with 32.8% of the vote, ahead of the CDU at 23.4%, the new BSW at 15.8% in its first state election, Die Linke at 13.1% and the SPD at 6.1%. The CDU, BSW and SPD then formed the first 'Brombeerkoalition' (minister-president Mario Voigt's cabinet) as a minority government without its own majority in the Landtag. For this record, these figures document the parliamentary power mix in which the AfD fraction pushed the motion to ban gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools and proposed dismantling the state's equality machinery, grounding the dossier's assessment of formal, multi-layered institutional hostility to gender policy.

records.name: Wales
records.current_summary:
Wales's devolved administration has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the UK's post-judgment years: the plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, with a dedicated young-people's edition posted January 2026.

Its 'Rights, Respect, Equality' statutory school guidance (consultation May 2025) obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on the grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, with incident recording and monitoring and a parental escalation route. The practical facility rules set state-wide are unchanged here, but the visible institutional commitment — maintained action plan, statutory recording duties — is an official posture of inclusion at a national moment of rollback.
records.current_localsOnly: The school guidance, young-people action-plan material and recording duties bear on resident families and pupils; for a short-term visitor they register only as a protective institutional climate.

sources.claim: Welsh Government LGBTQ+ Action Plan document for young people (posted January 2026): part of the standing devolved inclusion programme whose update page answers the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025.

Welsh Government statutory school guidance "Rights, Respect, Equality" (consultation May 2025): obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on sex, gender-reassignment and sexual-orientation grounds, with incident recording/monitoring and a parental escalation route.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales
sources.claim: Article on the Welsh Government's February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales, aiming to make Wales 'the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe'; it was announced in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 by Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement, built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel (March 2021) and a 12-week public consultation with 1,328 responses, and funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). It records the surrounding UK rollback — the UK Government blocking the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023 — while Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, with parents of transgender children calling for more help (BBC, March 2024). For this record: the official Welsh inclusion framework the summary describes, with dates and numbers.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wales
sources.claim: Overview article stating that LGBTQ rights in Wales track the UK framework: same-sex sexual activity legal since 1967 with the age of consent equalised in 2001 and remaining restrictions removed in 2003; the right to change legal gender since 2004 (Gender Recognition Act); civil partnerships since 2005 and same-sex marriage since 2014; full adoption rights since 2005; and discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Wales-specific practical content: trans adults were historically referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019 (BBC). For this record: confirms the legal framework and the local gender-identity clinic a trans visitor in Wales stands under.

records.name: Victoria
records.current_summary:
Victoria's Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025, created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, plus personal association; the civil grounds commenced 15 April 2026. The state human-rights commission's explainer records public incitement against a trans person becoming criminally chargeable alongside civil recourse.

A coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in Melbourne during the pandemic — lead case Bridget Flack, missing December 2020 — found Victoria Police failed the search, and Coroner Ingrid Giles made nine recommendations including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons risk practice; the government is reviewing them. The inquest documents a serious institutional failure; the 2025 legislation and the review process are the corrective response.
records.current_localsOnly: Prison-policy depth is largely resident-facing: Victorian LGBT prison protections are policy-based rather than legally enforceable (academic review), and the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities review mechanism binds public authorities over residents' service disputes.

sources.claim: Official factsheet (2025): Victoria's new anti-hate laws — the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025 passed in April 2025, inserting civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958 while repealing the RRTA; aimed at equal participation and public safety.

ABC News, 29 Aug 2024: a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people; the state government says it is reviewing the recommendations and local advocacy groups will press for implementation. Documents acute local risk factors (mental-health access) rather than visitor-facing law.

records.name: New South Wales
records.current_summary:
The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 (No. 19 of 2024, bipartisan, in force 4 April 2025) makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person interstate or overseas for the purpose or engaging a provider outside NSW. A civil complaints scheme runs through Anti-Discrimination NSW. NSW also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Against these strong legal protections, NSW carries a concentrated violence pattern. Kimberley McRae was killed in her Coogee apartment (January 2020); the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and the case went to murder trial (NSW Supreme Court), a positive institutional response. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old Filipina trans woman who had arrived in Australia approximately six weeks earlier, was strangled; her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that ABC reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in the same state within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents. NSW is a common-law state with no statutory bill of rights and no state-level anti-vilification offence comparable to Victoria's 2025 criminal provision.

Vs the national score of 0.86, NSW sits 0.02 below: the criminal conversion-practice ban and self-ID custody are strong positives but narrow in direct traveler-facing exposure (a typical tourist is unlikely to encounter a conversion-practice provider), while the violence-and-sentencing pattern is more relevant to a visitor's physical safety and shows both institutional capability (McRae murder trial) and institutional failure (Bruno 22-month sentence). Vs Victoria (0.88), which has the criminal vilification offence that NSW lacks, the two states trade different kinds of protection.

sources.claim: NSW Government media release, 4 April 2025: the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 takes effect — practices causing substantial mental or physical harm punishable by up to five years' jail, taking a person out of NSW for conversion therapy up to three years; Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways.

ABC Background Briefing, 2 Jul 2021: investigation into the killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines visiting Australia, in Wagga Wagga NSW; the perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term. Visitor-relevant: fatal violence against a trans woman traveller in NSW with a lenient custodial outcome.

records.name: Western Australia
records.current_summary:
WA's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute of "gender history," defined as a person who "identifies as a member of the opposite sex by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex." This is a narrower, medically-inflected, binary formulation than the "gender identity" language used in Victoria, Queensland and the federal Sex Discrimination Act. A non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may not meet the state-law definition and would rely solely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint. WA has no state anti-vilification offence (civil or criminal) and no statutory charter of rights binding public authorities.

Reform is underway: the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 received assent on 26 September 2024, removing medical and surgical prerequisites for registration of a sex or gender change, with substantive commencement by proclamation. This feeds back into the scope of "gender history" for complaints purposes but is not yet fully in force as of the scoring date.

Vs the national score of 0.86, WA sits 0.02 below: the narrower protective vocabulary and absence of both a vilification offence and a rights charter mean the state-level safety net is thinner than in eastern states, even though the federal floor is unchanged. Vs Queensland (national, no deviation record), which has a Human Rights Act 2019 binding public authorities and a conversion-practice prohibition in force since 2020, WA lacks both structural review and the specific coercion safeguard.
records.current_localsOnly: The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (assent 26 September 2024, substantive commencement still by proclamation) is a resident registration reform; until it is in force the state complaint definition still runs through certificates and registry changes rather than self-declared identity.

sources.claim: NOTE: consolidated PDF of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) was not retrievable at fetch time (state legislation portal blocks automated fetches); the companion official explainer below quotes the operative definitions - the Act protects the attribute 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex, with complaint eligibility tied to recognition certificates or registry change under the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework.

WA Government guidance (first published 6 Aug 2020, last updated 12 Feb 2026): gender history is a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) — a person has gender history if they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such; direct discrimination (including treating a person as their former sex) and indirect discrimination are unlawful.

sources.title: Reforms to remove barriers for LGBTQIA+ community | Western Australian Government
sources.claim: WA Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced on 16 April 2024 that the Births, Deaths, Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024 would be introduced to State Parliament that week, repealing the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishing the Gender Reassignment Board - which they say makes WA the only remaining Australian jurisdiction with such a board - in favour of a streamlined administrative process via the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Applicants would no longer need medical or surgical reassignment, providing instead a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling; a 'non-binary' sex descriptor would become available, stricter rules apply to under-18s (parental consent or Family Court of WA permission), and the Bill contains a statutory review clause after three years. The announcement implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations and links the reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a conversion-practices ban in 2025. This is the official government source for the record's claim that the 2024 Act removes medical and surgical prerequisites for registering a sex or gender change in Western Australia.

sources.title: Equal Opportunity Commission Fact Sheet - Gender Reassigned Person Discrimination | Western Australian Government
sources.claim: The WA Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet states that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (WA), recently passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, amends the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) at section 4(1) by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a new definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. It warns the amendment will not operate retrospectively and that 'gender history' discrimination complaints under the Equal Opportunity Act will need to be made in compliance with the new registration requirements once the Act commences, and notes the Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001. This primary government document confirms the record's claim that the 2024 reform feeds back into the scope of WA's 'gender history' attribute for complaints purposes and that substantive commencement is by proclamation.

sources.title: How to deal with gender discrimination and transphobia (WA) | Justice Connect
sources.claim: Justice Connect's WA-specific resource (last updated 16 April 2026) states that in Western Australia a discrimination complaint can be made to the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA), with a 12-month lodgement window, an acknowledgment of receipt within one week, and a free conciliation conference as the next step; it also details the alternative federal route - a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) within 24 months (12 months for employment matters) - noting only one route, state or federal, can be chosen. The resource names trans-specific local support in WA (TransFolk of WA, the Freedom Centre for under-26s). This confirms the record's claim that 'gender history' rather than 'gender identity' is the state-level protective attribute in WA and that state complaints run through the Equal Opportunity Commission.

freshness_all.fact: WA state government reforms announced 16 Apr 2024 remove barriers including surgery/medical requirements for identity-records changes; Equal Opportunity Act reforms remain in force per listed state sources.

records.name: Australian Capital Territory
records.current_summary:
The ACT Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, providing a legal review mechanism for a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or state facility that is absent in common-law states without a charter (NSW, WA, SA, TAS). The ACT is one of four Australian jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for the ACT. The absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and self-ID custody rule, places the territory modestly above the national average.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the ACT sits 0.02 above: the rights statute and self-identification custody are genuine structural positives for a visitor who might interact with police or detention, and no countervailing regional finding offsets them. Vs Victoria (0.88), the ACT lacks Victoria's 2025 criminal vilification offence but also lacks Victoria's coronial finding of police failure toward trans women; the two jurisdictions reach the same small positive deviation from different evidence.

sources.claim: ABC News, 3 Jul 2020: national survey of trans prisoners — experts estimate up to 400 trans and gender-diverse people in Australian cells, often inappropriately housed and at elevated risk of physical and sexual violence; NSW, Victoria, the ACT and Tasmania run explicit self-identification policies while QLD/NT/SA are unclear. ACT-relevant: names the ACT's explicit self-ID prison policy.

Human Rights Law Centre report 'Ending Strip Searching in Australian prisons' (2026, with trans-community group Flat Out and FIGJAM; only front matter and partial text retrieved): documents strip-searching practice and its disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners across Australian jurisdictions, underpinning how a detained gender-nonconforming visitor faces custody screening.

sources.title: Human Rights Act 2004 | Acts | ACT Legislation Register
sources.claim: The official ACT Legislation Register lists the Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) as In Force, with the current republished version and a full republication history back to 1 July 2004, and notes that under section 31 interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right; it also records uncommenced amendments by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025. This is the primary legal source for the record's claim that the ACT has its own Human Rights Act 2004 as the statutory rights framework public authorities must operate within.

sources.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
sources.claim: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. This is the first documented ACT-specific institutional-capacity finding and qualifies the record's claim that no countervailing region-specific finding was identified for the ACT.

sources.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
sources.claim: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. This dated ACT criminal statute supports the record's characterisation of the ACT as a protective rights jurisdiction and adds to the territory's structural positives beyond the Human Rights Act and self-identification custody rule.
